AccessExactly.reason: IDEA.md's purpose stated as exactly: no access without authorization, and access for whoever is signed in and authorized, so a system that refuses everyone fails it. Its three parts are the three rules of one admit decision (whose token, needs a grant, a grant lets in), and Lean shows each is needed.

content.statement: A user gets access to a resource exactly when they are signed in and authorized for it.
content.why: The idea says no one may access what they are not authorized to; and authorization is what lets a signed-in user in, or the system would serve no one. Who is authorized, and how a user signs in, the domain says below.

sources.formula: forall((u: User.T, r: Resource.T) => access(u, r) == (signedIn(u) && authorized(u, r)))

vocabulary: Resource: something a user may want to access
User: a person who uses the system
access: whether the system lets the user access the resource
authorized: whether the user is allowed the resource, by whatever rule the system adopts
signedIn: whether the user has signed in, so can present who they are
content.definition:
val accessExactly = Node.claim("AccessExactly",
  "A user gets access to a resource exactly when they are signed in and authorized for it.",
  why = "The idea says no one may access what they are not authorized to; and authorization is what lets a signed-in user in, or the system would serve no one. Who is authorized, and how a user signs in, the domain says below."
)(forall((u: User.T, r: Resource.T) => access(u, r) == (signedIn(u) && authorized(u, r))))
content.idea:
# Auth

A system decides which users may access which resources. No user may ever
access a resource they are not authorized to access.

Users identify themselves with tokens they receive at login. Authorization is
given by a table of grants: a user may access a path when a grant names that
user and that path.
content.notModelled:
- How tokens are issued at login, and when they expire.
- Who may change the table of grants.

AccessNeedsGrant.reason: IDEA.md: no user may ever access a resource they are not authorized to; here in terms of admitted requests and grants. It is the never-happen half of AccessExactly, and needed for it.

content.statement: A request is admitted on behalf of a user only if a grant names that user and the path.
content.why: No one may access what they are not authorized to, and a grant is what authorizes.

sources.formula: forall((t: String, p: Path) => admit(t, p).forall(u => grants.value.contains(Grant(u, p))))

vocabulary: admit: the system's decision on a request (a token and a path): the user it is admitted on behalf of, if any
grants: the grant table as stored when the request is decided
uses: case class Grant(user: UserId, path: Path)
content.definition:
val accessNeedsGrant = Node.claim("AccessNeedsGrant",
  "A request is admitted on behalf of a user only if a grant names that user and the path.",
  why = "No one may access what they are not authorized to, and a grant is what authorizes."
)(forall((t: String, p: Path) => admit(t, p).forall(u => grants.value.contains(Grant(u, p))))).under(accessExactly)

ClientAsserted.reason: Requests was chosen instead: The idea says users identify themselves with tokens; a client's own claim about who it is proves nothing. Revisit if requests come only from trusted services.

content.statement: A user has access to a path when a request naming that user is admitted on their behalf.
content.why: Simplest: the client says who it is, and the request carries that name. It trusts the client's claim about its identity.
substitutions: access := (u: UserId, p: Path) => admit(u.name, p) == Some(u)
vocabulary: access: whether the system lets the user access the resource
admit: the system's decision on a request (a token and a path): the user it is admitted on behalf of, if any

DecisionContract.reason: One call of admit meets all three rules at once, so it is a part of each and every running decision is checked against it. The admitted define is proven to meet it, and the five examples are the cases that matter: granted, not granted, someone else's token.

content.statement: A request is admitted on behalf of the user its token was issued to, exactly when a grant names that user and the path.
content.why: The three parts, stated for one call, so every result of the running system can be checked.

sources.post:
(token, path, decision) => decision.forall(u => sessions(token) == Some(u) && grants.value.contains(Grant(u, path))) &&
  sessions(token).forall(u => grants.value.contains(Grant(u, path)) ==> (decision == Some(u)))

examples: expect ("t1", Path("/a")) ⇒ Some(UserId("alice"))  given grants = List(Grant(UserId("alice"), Path("/a"))), sessions.bindTable(Map("t1" -> UserId("alice")))  — Alice's token and a grant for /a: she gets in
expect ("t1", Path("/b")) ⇒ None  given grants = List(Grant(UserId("alice"), Path("/a"))), sessions.bindTable(Map("t1" -> UserId("alice")))  — no grant for /b: refused
reject ("t1", Path("/b")) ⇒ Some(UserId("alice"))  given grants = List(Grant(UserId("alice"), Path("/a"))), sessions.bindTable(Map("t1" -> UserId("alice")))  — access without a grant is never given

reject ("t2", Path("/a")) ⇒ Some(UserId("alice"))  given grants = List(Grant(UserId("alice"), Path("/a"))), sessions.bindTable(Map("t1" -> UserId("alice")))  — a token that is not Alice's never acts for her
reject ("t1", Path("/a")) ⇒ None  given grants = List(Grant(UserId("alice"), Path("/a"))), sessions.bindTable(Map("t1" -> UserId("alice")))  — Alice with a grant for /a is not turned away
vocabulary: admit: the system's decision on a request (a token and a path): the user it is admitted on behalf of, if any
grants: the grant table as stored when the request is decided
sessions: the session table as stored when the request is decided: a token to the user it was issued to at login
uses: case class Grant(user: UserId, path: Path)
content.definition:
val decisionContract = Node.contract(admit)("DecisionContract",
  "A request is admitted on behalf of the user its token was issued to, exactly when a grant names that user and the path.",
  why = "The three parts, stated for one call, so every result of the running system can be checked."
)((token, path, decision) => decision.forall(u => sessions(token) == Some(u) && grants.value.contains(Grant(u, path))) &&
  sessions(token).forall(u => grants.value.contains(Grant(u, path)) ==> (decision == Some(u))))
  .under(tokenNamesHolder, accessNeedsGrant, grantLetsIn)
  .examples(grants.bind(List(Grant(UserId("alice"), Path("/a")))), sessions.bindTable(Map("t1" -> UserId("alice"))))(
    expect("t1", Path("/a"), Some(UserId("alice")), "Alice's token and a grant for /a: she gets in"),
    expect("t1", Path("/b"), None, "no grant for /b: refused"),
    reject("t1", Path("/b"), Some(UserId("alice")), "access without a grant is never given"),
    reject("t2", Path("/a"), Some(UserId("alice")), "a token that is not Alice's never acts for her"),
    reject("t1", Path("/a"), None, "Alice with a grant for /a is not turned away"))
content.implementation:
proven: admitted
admitted = (token: String, path: Path) =>
  sessions(token) match
    case Some(u) => if grants.value.contains(Grant(u, path)) then Some(u) else None
    case None    => None
runs: SessionStore(grants.value.toSet, sessions.value).decide

GrantLetsIn.reason: The can-do half of AccessExactly: a granted, signed-in user must get in, otherwise a server admitting no one would meet the safety rules. Lean shows it is needed.

content.statement: A request whose token was issued to a user with a grant for the path is admitted on their behalf.
content.why: A grant is there to be used: a system that turned a granted user away would meet the rules by serving no one.

sources.formula: forall((t: String, p: Path) => sessions(t).forall(u => grants.value.contains(Grant(u, p)) ==> (admit(t, p) == Some(u))))

vocabulary: admit: the system's decision on a request (a token and a path): the user it is admitted on behalf of, if any
grants: the grant table as stored when the request is decided
sessions: the session table as stored when the request is decided: a token to the user it was issued to at login
uses: case class Grant(user: UserId, path: Path)
content.definition:
val grantLetsIn = Node.claim("GrantLetsIn",
  "A request whose token was issued to a user with a grant for the path is admitted on their behalf.",
  why = "A grant is there to be used: a system that turned a granted user away would meet the rules by serving no one."
)(forall((t: String, p: Path) => sessions(t).forall(u => grants.value.contains(Grant(u, p)) ==> (admit(t, p) == Some(u))))).under(accessExactly)

GrantTable.reason: IDEA.md says it in these words: a user may access a path when a grant names that user and that path. A list of grants is that table and the simplest thing the server can store and search.

content.statement: A user is authorized for a path when a grant names that user and that path.
content.why: The idea defines authorization as a table of grants; who may change the table is not modelled.
substitutions: authorized := (u: UserId, p: Path) => grants.value.contains(Grant(u, p))
vocabulary: authorized: whether the user is allowed the resource, by whatever rule the system adopts
grants: the grant table as stored when the request is decided
uses: case class Grant(user: UserId, path: Path)

Identities.reason: The grant table names users by id and resources by path, so these are the identities the system can actually check; a richer user record would add nothing any rule reads.

content.statement: Users are named by ids, and resources are paths.
content.why: The grant table names users by id and resources by path, so these are what the system knows them by.
vocabulary: Resource: something a user may want to access
User: a person who uses the system

InMemorySessions.reason: Still one process deciding every request from tables held in memory; it governs the server code that runs DecisionContract's decision, so it sits under it. Revisit if the service runs as several instances.

content.statement: Sessions and grants are loaded into memory, in one process that decides every request.
content.why: One service decides access, and the tables fit in memory. A shared store would only be needed with several instances.
content.definition:
val inMemorySessions = Node.design(
  "InMemorySessions",
  "Sessions and grants are loaded into memory, in one process that decides every request.",
  why = "One service decides access, and the tables fit in memory. A shared store would only be needed with several instances."
)("src/main/scala/auth/Server.scala").under(decisionContract)

Requests.reason: The idea says users identify themselves with tokens; a client's own claim about who it is proves nothing. Revisit if requests come only from trusted services.

content.statement: A user has access to a path when some request for it is admitted on their behalf.
content.why: A user reaches a resource only through requests, and a request carries a token, not a user: the system sees tokens.
substitutions: access := (u: UserId, p: Path) => exists((t: String) => admit(t, p) == Some(u))
vocabulary: access: whether the system lets the user access the resource
admit: the system's decision on a request (a token and a path): the user it is admitted on behalf of, if any

SessionTable.reason: IDEA.md: users identify themselves with tokens they receive at login. A token-to-user table is what a login leaves behind, so signed in means some token maps to you; issuing and expiry stay out, as Not modelled says.

content.statement: A user is signed in when some session token was issued to them.
content.why: Users identify themselves with tokens they receive at login; the session table records which token was issued to whom. How tokens are issued is not modelled.
substitutions: signedIn := (u: UserId) => exists((t: String) => sessions(t) == Some(u))
vocabulary: sessions: the session table as stored when the request is decided: a token to the user it was issued to at login
signedIn: whether the user has signed in, so can present who they are

TokenNamesHolder.reason: A request carries a token, not a user: admitting it for anyone but the user the token was issued to would let one user in as another. It is the part of AccessExactly that ties access to being signed in, and Lean shows the root fails without it.

content.statement: A request is admitted only on behalf of the user its token was issued to.
content.why: A token stands for the user it was issued to: acting for anyone else would let one user in as another.

sources.formula: forall((t: String, p: Path) => admit(t, p).forall(u => sessions(t) == Some(u)))

vocabulary: admit: the system's decision on a request (a token and a path): the user it is admitted on behalf of, if any
sessions: the session table as stored when the request is decided: a token to the user it was issued to at login
content.definition:
val tokenNamesHolder = Node.claim("TokenNamesHolder",
  "A request is admitted only on behalf of the user its token was issued to.",
  why = "A token stands for the user it was issued to: acting for anyone else would let one user in as another."
)(forall((t: String, p: Path) => admit(t, p).forall(u => sessions(t) == Some(u)))).under(accessExactly)
